title: Kitty
pitch: Everyone's AI agent adds their own items and allergies to one shared group order — Kitty tracks it live and splits the bill automatically, no manual collecting or spreadsheet math needed.
about_excerpt: Everyone's AI agent adds their own items and allergies to one shared group order — Kitty tracks it live and splits the bill automatically, no manual collecting or spreadsheet math needed. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group orders always end the same way: one person becomes the unpaid dispatcher, allergies get missed, and the bill math takes longer than the meal did. We wanted agents to take over the boring parts — without losing what makes ordering together social. What it does Kitty is a shared order page where everyone's own AI agent adds their items and dietary restrictions straight into one live cart via WebMCP tools — no forms, no relaying your order through one exhausted human. The host locks the order in, and Kitty splits the bill automatically. How we built it Seven document.modelContext.registerTool() calls — browse_menu , add_item , remove_item , set_dietary_restriction , get_order_summary , split_bill , finalize_order — on a Next.js app on Vercel. Every mutating call is scoped server-side to the calling participant's identity, so an agent can only ever touch its own order. State lives in a lightweight session store, synced to every viewer with plain polling — no infrastructure we didn't need. Challenges we ran into Letting several independent agents write to one shared cart safely was the real problem. WebMCP's tool boundaries had to double as both a UX contract and a security boundary — otherwise a confused or malicious agent could overwrite someone else's order or invent a priced item that doesn't exist on the menu. Accomplishments that we're proud of Real multi-agent collaboration on one mutable session — not just one agent talking to one app — with guardrails (menu allow-lists, per-participant scoping, host-only finalize) tight enough we'd trust it with an actual office lunch order. What we learned WebMCP tools aren't just an API surface — they're a trust boundary. The moment more than one agent can touch the same state, "what should this tool refuse to do" matters as much as "what should it do." What's next for Kitty Itemized (not just equal) bill splitting, real restaurant menu imports, and letting a host's agent negotiate directly with a restaurant's own WebMCP tools once more storefronts expose them. Built With cloud firebase google in-memory-session-store react typescript web webmcp Try it out kitty-1003427733440.asia-south1.run.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by As a software architect with 16 years of experience, I led Kitty’s end-to-end architecture and technical execution. My contribution focused on turning the WebMCP concept into a secure, practical multi-agent ordering experience. I designed the system around seven purpose-built WebMCP tools for browsing the menu, adding and removing items, recording dietary restrictions, viewing the order, splitting the bill, and finalizing it. I treated every tool as both an application interface and a security boundary. I established the participant-scoped authorization model so each AI agent can modify only its owner’s items. I also designed host-only finalization, menu allow-list validation, participant tokens, and server-side allergy-conflict detection to prevent unauthorized or unsafe actions. To keep the hackathon implementation reliable and appropriately simple, I selected Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with lightweight REST endpoints and polling for live synchronization. I designed the in-memory session model and deployed the application to Google Cloud Run as a single-instance service, avoiding unnecessary infrastructure while preserving consistent shared state. Beyond architecture, I contributed to: - Product flow and interaction design - API and WebMCP tool contracts - Security and validation rules - Shared-order state management - Allergy and dietary-conflict detection - Automated bill splitting - Testing strategy and failure-case coverage - Cloud Run deployment architecture - Technical documentation and submission visuals support an actual group order.
